title: A coffee bean is a seed

layoutProps.alt: Rows of coffee shrubs on a green hillside at dawn, red cherries on their branches, shade trees behind.
layoutProps.lead: Before you serve a coffee, meet the fruit it comes from. By the end of this lesson you can tell a customer what a coffee bean is, and why the farm it grew on matters.

props.stem: Before you start: botanically, what is a coffee bean?

options.text: A legume, like a pea or a bean
options.feedback: A tempting guess from the name, but coffee is not a legume: the lesson shows what it really is.
Yes: the seed of a cherry. Keep it in mind as you read: everything that happens to that fruit shows in the cup.

options.text: A nut that grows in a hard shell
options.feedback: It does grow in a shell of sorts, the parchment, but inside a soft fruit: you will meet it below.

lines.markdown: Welcome to Fernhill! I train every new barista here, and I will walk you through this module.
The question customers ask most is *where does this coffee come from?* By Friday you will answer it in a sentence.

props.markdown:
Coffee grows in a belt around the equator, between the tropics, often on small, steep farms. Two species fill almost every cup: **arabica**, grown high up where the air is cool, and **robusta**, hardier, grown lower down in the heat.

Cool air slows the ripening of the cherries. That slower ripening is one reason high-grown arabica tastes sweeter and more complex.
props.aside: Robusta has about twice the caffeine of arabica. Roasters use it in espresso blends for its body and its crema.

props.alt: A mountain in two bands of farms: dark, upright arabica shrubs high on its slopes, broader robusta shrubs lower down, where it is warmer.
props.caption: High on the slope, often above 1,000 m: arabica. Lower down, in hotter air: robusta.

props.alt: A coffee cherry cut in half: a red skin, a pale layer of fruit, and two seeds side by side, each in a papery shell.
props.prompt: Select each marker to see what each layer of the cherry becomes.

items.title: The skin
items.markdown: Thin and red when ripe. In a washed coffee it comes off on the day of picking; in a natural it dries on the seed for weeks.

items.title: Pulp and mucilage
items.markdown: A sweet, sticky fruit, only a few millimetres thick. How much of it stays on the seed while it dries is what separates a washed, a honey and a natural coffee.

items.title: The parchment
items.markdown: A papery shell round each seed. It protects the bean while it dries and rests, and the dry mill removes it just before the coffee ships.

items.title: The bean
items.markdown: Two seeds facing each other, flat side to flat side, under a thin silverskin. Green and hard: this is the green coffee a roaster buys.

props.alt: The same coffee cherry cut in half, with four numbered zones on its layers.
props.stem: On this cherry, find the layer that the dry mill removes just before the coffee ships.

options.feedback: The skin comes off long before, at the wet mill or with the dried fruit of a natural.
The pulp goes before drying (washed) or with the dried fruit (natural), not at the end.
Yes: the parchment protects the bean until the dry mill hulls it, just before the green coffee is bagged.
The bean is what ships: everything around it is removed.
